title: RBA holds the cash rate at 4.10%, what it means for your mortgage and savings
excerpt: The Reserve Bank of Australia kept the cash rate on hold at 4.10% at its August meeting. We break down what that means for variable-rate borrowers, savers, and the broader economy.
body:
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) left the cash rate unchanged at 4.10% at its August meeting, the third hold in a row. The decision was widely expected, most economists had tipped no change after July's inflation print came in at 2.7%, comfortably inside the RBA's 2–3% target band.

In the accompanying statement, Governor Michele Bullock said the Board remains "data-dependent" and will need to see further confirmation that inflation is sustainably back at target before considering a cut. Wage growth is still running at around 3.7%, above the level the RBA considers consistent with the 2.5% midpoint of the target.

Markets are now pricing a 60% chance of a cut before Christmas, with the first move fully priced for early 2027.
whatItMeans: Variable-rate mortgage: Your monthly repayment does not change this month. If you have a $600,000 loan at an average 6.0% variable rate, you are paying roughly $3,598 a month, the same as last month.
Fixed-rate refinance: If your fixed rate is ending in the next 3–6 months, lenders are quietly trimming their 2- and 3-year fixed offers. Worth shopping around now before any cut.
Savers: Term deposit rates and bonus-saver accounts are unlikely to improve until the RBA actually cuts. The Big Four banks are still offering 4.5–5.0% on 12-month TDs.
First-home buyers: Serviceability buffers are still tight. Lenders test repayments at the customer rate + 3%, so today's rates are still restricting borrowing capacity.
